#768. Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't

Some people seem to attract mosquitoes wherever they go, but new research reveals that being a mosquito magnet depends on which species is doing the biting.

In a study published in iScience, researchers at Florida International University (FIU) tested how three of the world's most dangerous mosquito species responded to 119 human volunteers. Surprisingly, not a single participant attracted all three species. Instead, each species favored a different group of people, largely based on their individual body chemistry and natural skin odors.

The discovery could change how scientists approach the prevention of mosquito-borne diseases. Because different mosquito species respond to different chemical signals from human skin, researchers may eventually be able to create next-generation, species-specific repellents that offer more targeted protection.

"Isolating the components of human odor that attract or repel mosquitoes could lead to novel strategies to combat vector-borne diseases," said Matthew DeGennaro, a neurogeneticist who leads the research team and directs the Biomolecular Sciences Institute at FIU, Miami's state university.

Different Mosquito Species Prefer Different People

The researchers investigated three species responsible for spreading serious illnesses, including yellow fever, dengue, Zika, West Nile and other diseases. These were Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito) and Culex quinquefasciatus (southern house mosquito).

Led by Ph.D. student Kaylee Marrero, the investigation was the first to directly compare how several mosquito species reacted to the same human participants. The findings revealed unexpected differences in the chemical and microbial signals each species appeared to use when choosing whom to bite.

"We didn't expect the species to prefer different people when we started the study," Marrero said. "Each species having a distinct microbial signature that they use as a cue was so surprising to me."

Each mosquito species showed its own distinct preferences:

The Hidden Chemistry Behind Mosquito Attraction

Human body odor is far more complicated than it might seem. Our skin releases a mixture of more than 1,000 volatile organic compounds, many of which scientists have yet to fully identify or understand.

The researchers found that the three mosquito species did not share a common preference for particular individuals. Instead, each consistently favored its own subset of volunteers, suggesting that different species have evolved distinct methods for detecting and interpreting human scent.

To investigate what made certain people more appealing, the team collected samples of participants' body odors and skin microbiomes alongside the mosquito preference tests. They then examined which chemical compounds and microorganisms were present and measured their relative abundance.

The results showed strong connections between the mosquitoes' preferences and differences in the chemical and microbial makeup of people's skin.

"This connected so well with the differences in skin bacteria and odors," DeGennaro said. "It is clear to me now that our skin microbiomes define our human odor signature. Each species found its own way to decode that signature."

Could This Discovery Lead to Better Mosquito Repellents?

Understanding why one mosquito species finds a person attractive while another does not could open new possibilities for preventing dangerous infections.

By identifying the specific chemical compounds and skin bacteria that attract or discourage different mosquitoes, the FIU researchers are helping establish a scientific foundation for more precisely targeted repellents.

The findings could also improve public health strategies by allowing communities to focus on the particular mosquito species responsible for spreading disease in their region.

Rather than assuming that all mosquitoes are drawn to the same people for the same reasons, future prevention methods may be designed around the distinct chemical preferences of each species.

This Vampire Survivors spin-off has a lot of love for the famous grimdark sci-fi universe, but without the intimidatingly dense lore and complex systems.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We've had no shortage of great Warhammer 40K games lately, but most aren't exactly aimed at the casual crowd. Warhammer Survivors changes that, finally providing curious gamers with an easy entry point into the grim darkness of the 41st millennium.

Developed by Auroch Digital (in collaboration with Vampire Survivors' Poncle), this new spin on the survivors-like roguelite subgenre mixes the sci-fi 40,000 setting with the pure fantasy Age of Sigmar universe. This means heroes and enemies from all over the Warhammer mythos meet together in a bite-sized game that anyone can figure out and enjoy in less than five minutes.

When you look at the alternatives, that's a remarkable achievement for a franchise that's notoriously hard (and often expensive) to get into.

Warhammer Survivors isn't bogged down by dense lore, involved mechanics, or massive campaign playthroughs. It's more of an "inspired by" effort that gives casuals a small taste of the series' iconic characters — including Boltgun's Malum Caedo — and factions like the terrifying Tyranids, the raucous Orks, and the foul forces of Chaos.

All of 40K's (and Age of Sigmar's) recognizable elements are on display, but they serve more as flavoring sprinkled on top of Vampire Survivors' successful formula.

If you're new to the Survivors-like subgenre, it's a unique gaming experience. You battle an endless onslaught of enemies that slowly march towards you, with your character passively attacking automatically. You only need to move them around sprawling arenas and select level-up upgrades and items after collecting enough gems (skulls in this case).

The moment-to-moment gameplay is as simple as it can get outside of walking sims and interactive "experiences," but there's a deceiving depth to item synergies and how to correctly "build" characters to endure all the carnage.

Unlike Poncle's original game, Warhammer Survivors struggles a bit to get going. The early hours are sluggish until you unlock certain meta upgrades, but its still got that Vampire Survivors magic at its core.

As far as "podcast/gym games" go, this is a perfect fit. There's just enough going on to keep one's brain engaged, but minimal inputs and a tight overarching design lead to a rhythm that's easy to get into without using much brainpower. It's oddly satisfying to weave through enemies and level up your firepower, watching a single Astra Militarum grunt grow into a full Lasgun-spamming, chainsword-wielding wrecking ball.

Achievement and unlock hunters will find enough to bite into here, too. It's unclear if the devs will continue to add more Warhammer 40K and Age of Sigmar deep cuts to this game via DLCs and free updates, but those universes have daunting depths to explore. This really could become a gateway game for future 40K fans: by the time they realize they're hooked, they'll already have 2000 pts of space marines painted and ready to play.

As massive sci-fi and fantasy properties try to aggressively expand and absorb more and more fans, it's easy to pander to already-converted diehards too much. And sure, we can't wait for strategy heavyweights like Dawn of War 4 and Total War: WH40K either, but they're hardly good recommendations for folks who don't even know what a Space Marine is or why the robotic Necrons are so grumpy.

Warhammer Survivors won't answer those questions beyond the surface-level iconography, but it's fun enough to push those curious to dig deeper and embrace the same material in more mature video game genres... and maybe even pick up a few miniatures.

Warhammer Survivors is now available on PC (Steam & GOG), PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 1/2, and mobile (iOS & Android). It's also playable on Game Pass.

The third concert that Karol G was set to perform on Sunday (Nov. 15) at the Estadio GNP Seguros in Mexico City, as part of her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour, has been postponed to Tuesday (Nov. 17) “due to health reasons of the artist,” Ocesa announced on social media.

“This decision has been made prioritizing her health and well-being,” the promoter said in a statement. “After two nights full of music and special moments in Mexico City, we deeply regret not being able to share tonight with all the fans who were looking forward to joining her. Ocesa informed fans that tickets previously purchased for Sunday’s concert will be valid for the new date, so no changes are necessary. Those who wish to request a refund can do so through Ticketmaster.

On Friday (November 13), the “Bichota” singer performed the first of her three concerts at the iconic stadium in Mexico City, where Thalia made a surprise guest appearance to sing a duet of “Piel Morena,” “Amor a la Mexicana” and “¿A Quién Le Importa?” The performance marked the return of the iconic Mexican singer and actress to the stages of Mexico City after a decade.

#764. Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts

Some of Europe's most famous medieval manuscripts, including the York Gospels, have revealed an extraordinary secret hidden in their pages. Scientists have discovered ancient viral DNA preserved in the animal skins used to make parchment, opening a new window into the 3,500-year history of sheeppox virus (SPPV).

The discovery was made by an international research team led by University College Dublin (UCD). By analyzing parchment from centuries-old documents, the researchers uncovered the first genetic evidence that this destructive disease was spreading through European sheep flocks long before modern times.

Sheeppox is highly contagious and can spread through a flock with alarming speed. It can kill large numbers of infected animals, particularly young sheep, while also causing major economic losses by reducing wool, meat, and milk production.

Ancient Manuscripts Preserve the DNA of Deadly Viruses

Published in Science Advances, the new study reconstructs more than 3,500 years of sheeppox virus evolution. Researchers identified viral DNA in several historically important medieval manuscripts, revealing that documents preserved for their cultural significance can also contain valuable biological evidence.

Among the manuscripts examined was the 1,000-year-old York Gospels, considered one of the finest surviving illuminated manuscripts from the early Anglo-Saxon period. The researchers also studied older works, including the Corpus Glossary at Corpus Christi College Cambridge, one of the earliest English dictionaries, along with other medieval manuscripts from Britain and continental Europe.

The secret lies in the parchment itself. Before paper became widely available, manuscripts were often produced using carefully prepared animal hides, including skins from sheep, goats, and cattle. These materials can preserve traces of an animal's biological history, including evidence of infections present when it died.

In several manuscripts, the researchers detected sheeppox virus DNA on multiple pages. These findings indicate that infected animals had supplied some of the skins used to produce the documents.

An especially surprising discovery involved viral DNA found on parchment made from calfskin and goatskin. Because sheeppox primarily infects sheep, the results raise two possibilities: the virus may occasionally have infected other livestock species, or viral material may have contaminated the skins during parchment production.

Historic Books Become Unexpected Disease Archives

"The recording of ancient DNA of pathogens has completely changed our understanding of infectious disease in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve animal pathogen DNA. It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past," said Louis L'Hôte, PhD candidate at UCD and lead author of the study.

"These genomes help us understand how these pathogens evolved and how they impacted past societies -- such as sheeppox virus, which we show has been affecting Eurasian sheep herds for at least three and a half millennia."

The findings suggest that libraries and archives may hold far more information about historical diseases than previously recognized. Manuscripts that have survived for hundreds of years could provide genetic evidence of livestock outbreaks that left few other records.

"Parchment making has been considered a vanishing craft, but we are beginning to understand just how much of the past it has retained. This project shows that parchments not only preserve our cultural history for hundreds of years, but also the landscape of disease in our livestock in the medieval period," said Dr. Kevin G. Daly, Associate Professor at UCD School of Agriculture and Food Science and the study's supervising author.

"This kind of exciting, surprising discovery is only possible when researchers from a range of disciplines come together to share their expertise and data -- a generosity and trust that collaborative science depends on."

The project brought together specialists in genetics, history, virology, protein chemistry, and conservation, allowing the team to investigate the manuscripts from both historical and biological perspectives.

Ancient Sheep Teeth Reveal 3,700 Years of Disease

The medieval manuscripts were only part of the investigation. To trace the disease further into the past, the scientists also examined DNA recovered from sheep teeth dating to the Bronze Age.

Teeth are particularly useful for studying ancient infections because they can protect genetic material for thousands of years, often preserving evidence that has disappeared from other skeletal remains.

The researchers identified the oldest known genetic traces of sheeppox virus in sheep teeth recovered from ancient pastoralist settlements in the Eurasian steppe. When combined with the manuscript findings, this evidence shows that the disease has affected livestock for more than 3,700 years.

To investigate how the virus developed, the team compared ancient viral DNA with genetic sequences from modern viruses. Their analysis suggests that the main branches of the capripoxvirus family (sheeppox virus, goatpox virus, and lumpy skin disease virus) separated from one another sometime between 11,500 and 3,700 years ago.

That estimated timeline coincides with major changes in human history, including the domestication of livestock and the large-scale movement of sheep from the Eurasian steppe into Europe. These movements may have played an important role in the virus's long history of transmission.

A Deadly Virus That Has Barely Changed in Thousands of Years

One of the study's most striking findings was how little the sheeppox virus has changed genetically over the past several thousand years. Unlike some other viruses, its genome appears to have remained remarkably stable despite its long history of infecting livestock.

Understanding that stability could help scientists identify the genetic changes that originally allowed the virus to become an effective sheep pathogen.

The discovery also has immediate relevance. Sheeppox remains a serious threat to livestock farming, with outbreaks continuing to cause substantial economic damage.

"People around the world are still fighting against this pathogen -- there is currently an outbreak of sheeppox in Greece, causing much economic damage," said Louis L'Hôte.

"Ancient genomes can help us understand how these pathogens affecting us today evolved. We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia."

L'Hôte added: "This might mean that genetic changes before this point were very important to how the sheeppox virus evolved to infect its host, which may help us fight the pathogen in the future."

By uncovering viral DNA in both medieval manuscripts and prehistoric animal remains, the researchers have demonstrated a powerful new way to investigate the history of infectious diseases. Their work suggests that materials preserved for entirely different purposes may contain valuable clues about the emergence, spread, and evolution of pathogens that continue to affect the world today.

The research was funded by Taighde Éireann-Research Ireland and the European Research Council. Led by UCD, the project involved more than 30 institutions in Ireland and internationally, including Trinity College Dublin, the Helmholtz Institute for One Health, Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, the University of Leicester, Cambridge University, and the University of Copenhagen.

SpaceX's Starship megarocket is slated to launch on its ambitious 15th flight test as soon as this Friday (Nov. 13). Will you be able to spot its leviathan upper stage, known as Ship, or its Starlink satellite passengers as they circle Earth during the historic orbital jaunt?

Flight 15's 75-minute launch window opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) on Nov. 13. Starship will fly from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, where it will be 4:45 p.m. at the opening of the window — about an hour before sunset. The launch could therefore be especially dramatic for folks in the area.

"As it launches towards the southeast, and it will be daylight, then the prospects for viewing from the U.S. are going to be in Texas and the states along the Gulf of Mexico," Robert Massey, deputy executive director at the Royal Astronomical Society, told Space.com. "They could see the exhaust plume (the 'jellyfish') with the sky darker for observers further east."

If all goes to plan, Starship's Super Heavy booster will propel the Ship upper stage through the densest part of Earth's atmosphere before returning to Starbase for a powered landing and capture via the "chopstick" arms of the "Mechazilla" tower system. Ship, meanwhile, will go on to orbit Earth approximately 14 times over the following 22 hours, during which time it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites before returning to Starbase for its own ambitious catch attempt.

Satellite visibility in the night sky depends on a cocktail of factors, from the size of the spacecraft to its reflectivity, orbital inclination and position relative to the Earth and sun.

Ship is big — about 171 feet (52 meters) tall — so it will be a viable target for skywatchers, experts say.

"It certainly will be visible in twilight hours. It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size," professor James Osborn of Durham University told Space.com. "Where and when is a bit more tricky."

Ship and its Starlink satellites may be seen in the 90 minutes directly after sunset on Nov. 13 and before sunrise on Nov. 14, as the probes catch the sunlight on either side of Earth's colossal shadow as they drift through the twilight sky.

The spacecraft will initially appear as a string of bright, evenly spaced lights, with Ship most likely appearing significantly brighter than the Starlink satellites. However, Osborn noted that the lack of publicly available data makes it challenging to forecast exactly when the spacecraft will appear.

"During its 14 orbits over 22 hours, the spacecraft is between inclinations of 30.5 [degrees] N and S of the equator," explained Massey. "So it will be best viewed between those latitudes, and then lower in the sky up to latitudes of 40 N and 40 S. That's pretty much the whole of the contiguous U.S."

Space.com skywatching columnist and veteran meteorologist Joe Rao shared further details on what stargazers may see with the naked eye as Ship drifts silently through the autumn sky.

"When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station, but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," explained Rao. "The Starlink V3 satellites are much smaller, so not as bright, perhaps ranging anywhere from 2nd to 4th magnitude, depending on the angle of illumination with reflected light from the sun."

Magnitude is the scale used by astronomers to measure the brightness of objects in the night sky. The lower the magnitude, the brighter the object! The unaided eye can make out objects with a magnitude of around +6.5 under ideal dark sky conditions, while the planet Venus currently shines at magnitude -4.41.

The Starlink train will likely fall further behind Starship as the 22-hour mission progresses, while the train itself will become more elongated, according to Rao. "For locations where it will make a high arc across the sky, the Starship should be visible for at least a few minutes, although because it is orbiting at a lower altitude (170 miles/275 km) compared to the ISS, it probably will appear to move somewhat faster. "

There are multiple handy resources that should allow you to track Ship and the newly deployed batch of V3 Starlink satellites following their scheduled launch on Nov. 13, including the websites Heavens-Above, Star Dash, Orbital Radar and Find Starlink.

Be sure to keep an eye on our Starship Flight 15 live blog for all the latest news along with our launch timings article containing details on how to watch SpaceX's potentially historic orbital launch attempt.

Editor's Note: If you capture a photo of Starship and want to share it with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

#761. DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets

Scientists have uncovered a remarkable collection of DNA hidden within the Shroud of Turin, revealing a surprisingly complex biological history behind one of the world's most mysterious and controversial religious artifacts. The genetic evidence includes traces of humans, bacteria, fungi, plants, animals, and even Mediterranean red coral, offering new clues about the environments and people that have come into contact with the famous cloth over the centuries.

Published in Scientific Reports, the study used advanced DNA sequencing technology to examine samples collected from the Shroud in 1978. For the first time, researchers applied a sophisticated technique (rigorous PCR-free next-generation metagenomic sequencing) to these officially collected samples, allowing them to identify genetic material preserved within the linen fibers in unprecedented detail.

Unlike traditional DNA testing, which often focuses on genetic material from a single organism, metagenomic sequencing can detect DNA from many different species within the same sample. This makes it particularly useful for studying historical objects that have been handled, stored, and exposed to changing environments over long periods.

By examining this genetic material, the international research team assembled what they describe as the most comprehensive picture yet of the biological traces accumulated on the Shroud throughout its history.

Human DNA and a Hidden World of Microorganisms

Among the discoveries were multiple lineages of human mitochondrial DNA, suggesting that genetic material from different human populations has accumulated on the cloth. Mitochondrial DNA is a small portion of our genetic material that is inherited through the maternal line, making it especially useful for studying ancestry and population history.

The researchers also identified an unexpectedly diverse microbiome, the collection of microscopic organisms associated with a particular environment or object. These included bacteria commonly found on human skin, various fungi, and microorganisms adapted to living in salty environments.

Some of these organisms belong to a group known as archaea, which are single-celled microorganisms distinct from bacteria. Certain archaea can thrive in extremely salty conditions that would be difficult for many other forms of life to tolerate.

Together, these findings reveal that the Shroud carries a complicated biological record shaped by repeated human contact and exposure to different environmental conditions.

DNA From Plants, Animals, and Mediterranean Coral

The discoveries extended far beyond human DNA and microorganisms. Scientists also detected genetic traces from numerous plant and animal species, adding another layer to the Shroud's biological history.

Plant DNA included cultivated wheat, carrots, maize, bananas, and peanuts. Genetic material from domesticated animals was also present, including cattle, pigs, chickens, dogs, and cats.

One particularly unusual finding was DNA associated with Mediterranean red coral.

The wide variety of biological material suggests that the cloth has encountered a diverse range of living organisms and environmental influences. These genetic traces may reflect its long history of handling, storage, and movement through different geographical regions.

Importantly, the presence of DNA from a particular species does not establish when that material reached the cloth. Some traces could have accumulated relatively recently, while others may reflect much older interactions. This makes the findings valuable for reconstructing the Shroud's environmental history, but also highlights the difficulty of interpreting DNA recovered from an object that has been exposed to human activity for centuries.

Can DNA Solve the Mystery of the Shroud of Turin?

Despite the remarkable diversity of genetic material, the researchers emphasize that their findings cannot establish the Shroud's age or authenticity.

The Shroud of Turin is a linen cloth bearing the faint image of a human figure and has long been associated by some believers with the burial of Jesus. Its origins have been debated for generations, making it one of the most extensively investigated historical and religious artifacts in the world.

Because the cloth has been touched and exposed to different environments over many centuries, its DNA represents a mixture of biological material accumulated at different times. This makes it impossible to reliably separate any original DNA that might have been associated with the fabric from the many genetic traces deposited afterward.

Instead, the research demonstrates how modern forensic genomics and proteomics can reveal information that traditional methods might miss. Forensic genomics uses genetic evidence to investigate biological origins and interactions, while proteomics examines proteins, which can also preserve valuable clues about biological materials.

Together, these approaches offer powerful new ways to investigate how historical objects have been preserved, handled, and exposed to different environments.

Modern DNA Technology Reveals New Historical Clues

Professor Noemi Procopio, Professor of Forensic Science at the University of Lancashire, contributed to the international research collaboration. She emphasized that advances in forensic technology are making it possible to recover information from historical samples collected decades earlier.

Professor Noemi Procopio, Professor of Forensic Science at the University of Lancashire, said: "The Shroud of Turin continues to fascinate historians, scientists and the public, and we're thrilled to reveal new information about the biological complexity preserved within samples collected almost 50 years ago by applying new cutting-edge forensic DNA technologies.

"The Shroud represents a rich archive of genetic information that has accumulated over centuries of human interaction and environmental exposure. While the DNA evidence cannot answer all the questions about the age or authenticity of the cloth, it provides novel insights into its biological history and demonstrates how advances in forensic science can unlock new information from historical artifacts."

Materials provided by University of Lancashire. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#760. Gracie Abrams Sets 2027 Australian Arena Shows for ‘Look at My Life Tour’

The singer-songwriter will play three nights each in Melbourne and Sydney next July and August, with Arlo Parks as a special guest

Gracie Abrams is bringing The Look at My Life Tour to Australia next year.

Abrams will play six arena shows across two cities in July and August 2027: three nights at Melbourne’s Rod Laver Arena on July 27, 28 and 30, followed by three at Sydney’s Afterpay Arena on Aug. 3, 4 and 6. British singer-songwriter Arlo Parks will open all six dates.

“Australia! I’ve missed you so much and I cannot express just how excited I am to return to Melbourne and Sydney next July/August for ‘The Look at My Life Tour,’” Abrams said in a statement. “A show that we’ve been working very hard to put together, a show that we hope you love as much as we do.” Related Daniel Hall, Co-Founder of Australian Rock Band Taxiride, Dies at 48 U2 Opens 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Ceremony With Surprise Performance Phil Collins Tells Rock Hall Crowd: 'You Haven't Heard the Last of Me' Explore Arlo Parks Gracie Abrams See latest videos, charts and news

“I’ve just missed you so much more than I can tell you… as soon as I heard for sure we were coming back my heart began to sing,” she added. “I will see you soon, I love you so much… we’re gonna make it great.”

The tour supports Daughter From Hell, Abrams’ third studio album, which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 in July with 124,000 equivalent album units, her first chart-topping album. Produced with longtime collaborator Aaron Dessner, it also reached No. 1 in Australia. A deluxe edition arrives Friday (Nov. 20) with five additional tracks, including “Out of Nowhere,” which she first performed at Glastonbury in 2025, and “Crazy Girl,” previously available only on vinyl. The Look at My Life Tour launches Dec. 2 in Denver.

The run marks Abrams’ third visit to Australia in four years. She sold out six theater shows on her first trip in January 2024, then returned in 2025 for 11 arena dates across Sydney, Brisbane, Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth on The Secret of Us Tour. This time she is concentrating on two markets.

The Secret of Us (2024) debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200, and its deluxe edition produced “That’s So True,” her first top 10 hit on the Billboard Hot 100. Her Taylor Swift collaboration “us.” earned a Grammy nomination for best pop duo/group performance. Abrams will also make her acting debut in the upcoming A24 film Please.

An artist presale begins Wednesday (Nov. 18) at 10 a.m. local time, followed by Frontier Touring and Live Nation presales Thursday (Nov. 19). General sale opens Friday (Nov. 20) at 10 a.m. local time.

#759. Pitch Perfect: The 20 Best Music Schools in the World

From Juilliard and USC to Berklee and Eastman, these are the programs and conservatories training the next generation of Hollywood composers.

Conservatories, typically built around intensive studio training in performance and composition rather than the broad general education requirements of a traditional college, made a strong showing in THR‘s annual look at the world’s best music schools. But schools with well-regarded media scoring programs, which teach composing for film, TV, video and gaming — USC Thornton, Eastman, Berklee and Columbia Chicago — retain their influence in Hollywood and beyond.

David Serkin Ludwig, dean and director of the music division at Juilliard, which continues to expand its opportunities for media scoring, says that the grounding conservatories give their students is important in a world where AI is encroaching even on creative disciplines like music. “A great hedge against the replacement aspect of AI is having a very deep and thorough training, because you want depth of knowledge and experience for people using the tools,” he says. “So I’m happy with the direction we’re going, and we just have to keep staying current.” Related Stories Music Richard Sterban, Oak Ridge Boys' Bass Singer, Dies at 83 Music Meet Plave, the Very Real Virtual K-pop Boy Group

To see where that type of training is happening, we turned to the people working in the field. Contributing to this year’s ranked list via survey: the Society of Composers and Lyricists, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ music branch, the Alliance for Women Film Composers and the Composers Diversity Collective. Thanks go to Ray Costa and Costa Communications for their help in distributing THR‘s survey.

Long a holdout on media scoring instruction, Juilliard now offers several courses, including Composing for Visual Media, which gives students the fundamental skills they need to compose for film and TV, as well as commercials and video games, with focuses on both traditional and more diverse contemporary approaches. Scoring to Picture is a two-credit course offered through the school’s extension division that covers spotting, or placement of music and sound in a project, scoring brief media excerpts and enhancing drama in film with music.

The school also has renovated and upgraded its film scoring labs and classrooms. “We’re aspiring to stay on the cutting edge of available technologies for them, so we’re doing a lot in interactive music technology as well,” says Serkin Ludwig, the dean and director of the music division. “So looking into motion sensors, other kinds of digital response tools but also just the software itself, and making platforms available for our students: laptops, cameras, all the devices and tools they need to create their own media.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI John Williams (Star Wars); Philip Glass (The Hours)

USC Thornton continues to thrive at the center of the Hollywood music community and offers a two-semester master’s degree program in screen scoring that recruits about 20 students a year for a deep dive into composition, orchestration, programming, conducting, producing and editing music for screen-based media. The program has been chaired by Jeanine Cowen since 2022. “We’re really trying to take advantage of our relationship with the cinema school,” Cowen says. “In September, we did a massive mock scoring session with 25 Thornton musicians and our composers, and we were just doing it so everybody could get a sense of what a scoring session is. The filmmakers are amazed because most of them have no idea what a live ensemble can do for their picture. So we’ll probably keep doing that because it was such a huge success.”

While Los Angeles has faced challenges in employment and keeping jobs in town, Cowen says Hollywood’s creative culture is still vital: “Every session we’ve had so far, the pro studio players are all busy, so we’re not able to get our first call all the time, and it’s because there’s a lot going on in town that’s keeping musicians busy.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Bear McCreary (The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power); James Newton Howard (The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes)

University of Rochester’s Eastman School of Music continues to offer students both intensive conservatory training in performance and composition, as well as a renowned program for film and media scoring with funding and participation from prolific composer Jeff Beal (House of Cards, Monk) for the school’s Beal Institute for Film Music and Contemporary Media. Next year will see the school broaden the institute’s approach, as associate professor of music and technology Dennis DeSantis explains: “In an ever-evolving technological world, Eastman’s Beal Institute for Film Music and Contemporary Media is excited to reach beyond the traditional methods of composition by launching a new major in music creation and technology in fall 2027. With this program, we invite technologically curious musicians to explore new ways of creating and experiencing music, keeping Eastman’s world-class curriculum at the forefront of musical innovation.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Maria Schneider (Grammy-winning composer); Lew Soloff (jazz trumpeter)

Sean McMahon continues in his role as chair of screen scoring at Berklee, which includes two programs, Film and Media Scoring and Game and Interactive Media Scoring, both of which are four-year bachelor of music degrees. The school’s Next Gen Composer Lab is an immersive, five-day collaboration among Berklee Screen Scoring, the Boston Conservatory and the Vienna Symphonic Library. “Nine composers each get to conduct and record their original music with the 84-piece Vienna Synchron Orchestra, while two elite conservatory instrumentalists sit inside the orchestra itself, recording shoulder to shoulder with Europe’s finest session players,” McMahon says.

Berklee now also offers a Master of Arts in music supervision, the first of its kind in the world: a one-year, fully online graduate program covering the art of selecting, licensing and integrating music into TV, games and advertising and taught by music supervisor pros like Julia Michels (The Devil Wears Prada).

NOTABLE ALUMNI Alex Lacamoire (Tony winner for Hamilton); Howard Shore (The Lord of the Rings)

The Herb Alpert School offers media scoring training through its composition and theory program, in which student composers receive instruction in studio recording, counterpoint, global musicianship and orchestration. Students are encouraged to take advantage of interdisciplinary crossovers to collaborate with live performers, student film and media directors, and cross-cultural ensembles inspired by ethnomusicology and world jazz styles. New students must complete a music theory assessment examination to achieve placement in global musicianship and formal music theory classes.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Joseph Trapanese (The Greatest Showman); Quincy Jones (Thriller)

If you’re extremely talented, looking for premier conservatory training in the Los Angeles area and hard up for cash, Colburn offers elite undergraduate, graduate and postgraduate programs that concentrate on classical performance and repertoire — and a generous price break. All students receive a full-tuition scholarship and grants that cover room and board. Undergraduate programs include a four-year bachelor of music degree that offers studio performance training and courses on musical theory, music history, ear training and the humanities, with students completing both junior and senior solo recitals. The Performance Diploma is a four-year nondegree program for students with ambitions of professional performance but who do not yet have a bachelor’s degree. It’s essentially courses in theory, performance and ear training without the humanities requirements. Colburn also offers graduate programs including a two-year master of music with a focus on high-level instrumental mastery and advanced seminars in music history, theory and composition.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Kris Bowers (Bridgerton); Elias Peter Brown (conductor)

Royal College of Music offers a master’s degree in composition with a specialism in composition for screen — an advanced program that trains composers for professional careers through workshops, master classes, performance projects and collaborations with professional artists. The program is tailored to individual student needs and ambitions, with instruction from world-class professors and visiting artists. Electives include classes in orchestration, experimental music, conducting, music education, analysis and practical skills to keep students up to speed with constantly evolving digital technology and global perspectives. The school’s exchange program allows students to audition for the chance to study abroad during the fall term of their second year at the school.

Each year, the school hosts a Composition for Screen Showcase featuring a live ensemble performing music written by students accompanying films projected on the big screen; it’s attended by the public and industry professionals.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Andrew Lloyd Webber (The Phantom of the Opera); James Horner (Titanic)

In addition to its venerable Ivy League name, Yale boasts proximity to New York, Boston and the town of New Haven, giving students a rich cultural and artistic environment in which to take advantage of the school’s prestigious conservatory training. Yale offers a master of music, master of musical arts, doctor of musical arts and artist diploma in composition, with courses taught by concert hall composers including Katherine Balch, Martin Bresnick and Aaron Jay Kernis. While the school does not offer degree programs in media scoring, Yale’s Center for Collaborative Arts and Media helps students combine music with film, video, computer science and the visual arts. Yale’s Center for Studies in Music Technology provides students with a sophisticated recording studio and computer lab featuring software for acoustic and electroacoustic music. All students receive scholarships that cover $42,000 in tuition fees.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Marco Beltrami (Logan); David Lang (2008 Pulitzer winner)

Curtis offers a mix of liberal arts education and conservatory training focused on instrumental performance. Foundational Studies teaches students the basics in intervals and chords, notation conventions, tuning systems, scales and modes, and various musical forms. Required courses include studies in musical cultures of the world, a survey of 20th and 21st century music techniques, as well as improvisation and electives including musical history. All students receive scholarships that cover $55,995 in tuition fees.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Leonard Bernstein (West Side Story); Jennifer Higdon (2010 Pulitzer winner for Violin Concerto)

NEC’s five-year bachelor/master’s programs allow students to combine their conservatory training with academic programs from partnering institutions Harvard College or College of the Holy Cross, earning a bachelor’s degree from those schools as well as a master of music degree at NEC over a five-year period. Undergraduate students interested in media scoring can take a music technology concentration that includes classes in scoring for new media; performance with electronics or multimedia; recording and mixing; and algorithmic music. Contemporary improvisation programs delve into film music styles and techniques like film noir ensembles and cross-genre interdisciplinary scoring.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Stephanie Economou (Assassin’s Creed Valhalla: Dawn of Ragnarök); Coretta Scott King (classically trained soprano)

Oberlin doesn’t offer a dedicated media scoring program, but it nonetheless has created an excellent environment in which to learn many of the skill sets and technologies that can make students into effective composers for film, games or commercials. Their TIMARA (Technology in Music and Related Arts) program teaches electronic music and sound design, computer music and multichannel media productions. The school’s Cinema and Media department is housed in the Danny DeVito & Rhea Perlman Center for Media Education and Production above the Apollo Theatre and offers production courses, film labs and soundstages that afford conservatory musicians ample room to perform student compositions.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Jeremy Denk (pianist); Claire Chase (flutist)

Columbia College Chicago School of Audio and Music continues its comprehensive two-year MFA program, run by graduate program director Kubilay Uner for the past 12 years, and it has recently added an undergraduate Bachelor of Arts in music composition for media, led by Lee Sanders, nine-time BMI Award winner and composer for CBS’ The Amazing Race.

Uner has 15 students in his first-year program and 14 in the second year and says that the highly selective MFA will remain much the same as it has been in recent years. The school also is welcoming BAFTA-nominated composer Sam Hulick (video game Mass Effect) to the MFA program’s faculty. “Many in our community know Sam from his work as the owner of ReelCrafter, which is the No. 1 platform for people to put their pitch reels together in our industry,” says Uner.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Tomás Videla (The House of the Spirits); Batu Sener (Ice Age: Boiling Point)

MSM coursework includes classes like composition forum, instrumentation and orchestration, electronic music, form and analysis, and score reading. The school’s studio facilities include the Jean Lignel Electronic Music Studio and labs, which provide digital audio workstation tools including Pro Tools, Logic and Digital Performer, as well as virtual instruments, MIDI protocol and multitrack production techniques. MSM also offers an introductory film scoring course in its pre-college curriculum, a Saturday program for students from 8 to 18 years old.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Angelo Badalamenti (Twin Peaks); John Corigliano (The Red Violin)

Established more than 100 years ago, Frost is well known for its innovative curriculum, award-winning faculty and focus on real-world industry experience. Its Media Scoring and Production program, led by newly appointed department chair Camilo Rodriguez, combines composition, orchestration, digital audio production and hands-on studio experience with mentorship from accomplished industry professionals, including Grammy-winning and three-time Emmy-winning composer Carlos Rafael Rivera (The Queen’s Gambit, Hacks).

NOTABLE ALUMNI Pat Metheny (Grammy-winning musician); Ben Folds (musician)

NYU Steinhardt’s Screen Scoring program, operated out of the Department of Music & Performing Arts, was founded and is currently run by Ronald H. Sadoff, Ph.D. “Steinhardt’s Screen Scoring program trains screen composers to think of themselves as filmmakers and storytellers at the [bachelor’s, master’s] and Ph.D. levels,” Sadoff says. “Taking advantage of all that New York City offers, students collaborate on more than 500 projects each year with peers from film and media schools, including NYU Tisch Film and Television, the NYU Game Center and Columbia University’s film school.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Gavin Brivik (The Pitt); Ariel Marx (Dying for Sex)

CalArts offers a bachelor of fine arts in music with a specialization in composition through its Music Composition and Experimental Sound Practices program, run by Michael Pisaro-Liu. The category includes film and media scoring, among other elements, but according to Pisaro-Liu, the school has plans to offer a minor in film and media scoring starting in 2027. “It’s an art school environment, all in one building, which means that the School of Music is housed right next to schools of Arts, and Film and Video, along with theater and what we call critical studies and dance,” Pisaro-Liu says. “So it’s an environment that is, in its very nature, multimedia or across media, and film music students are in classes with art majors, film majors, dance majors and so forth. Here, your cohorts are people who are going on to become animators and filmmakers. So that’s one thing about the CalArts environment that is different from other schools.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Michael Skloff (Friends); Raven Chacon (2022 Pulitzer winner)

Located near Silicon Valley and California’s hub of video game production, SFCM’s Technology and Applied Composition (TAC) program offers bachelor of music, master of music and professional studies certificates with tracks in film scoring, game scoring and sound design. Students learn writing and producing music for live instruments, working with ensembles ranging from solo instrumentalists to small chamber sized. The ultimate goal is for students to work individually with film directors on short films, documentaries or longer-form narrative productions.

NOTABLE ALUMNI John Adams (composer/ conductor); Isaac Stern (violinist)

While established in 1977 as the Guitar Institute of Technology and promoted initially as a school for rock ‘n’ rollers, the Musicians Institute has leveraged its location in the heart of Hollywood to make it a popular destination for musicians and composers eager to break into the film industry. Director of performance studies Daniel Levin runs the school’s media and film scoring program, which offers a bachelor’s degree in the discipline. “It’s super comprehensive,” Levin says of the program. “Students study the full gamut of theory, ear training and counterpoint orchestration.” Students ultimately complete a capstone project where they record their compositions with a studio orchestra. “Not only do they compose it, but they have to set up the Pro Tools session, to prep all the music and conduct,” Levin says. “If they do everything that they need to do according to our program, they’re pretty well set to go out and succeed in the field.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Cody Matthew Johnson (Star Wars Outlaws)

Located in the San Fernando Valley, Cal State Northridge is a friendly and tremendously affordable alternative to many of the area’s better-known schools, with a reputation for preparing students for practical careers. The school’s Mike Curb College of Arts, Media, and Communication offers a bachelor of music in commercial and media writing that combines classical and jazz orchestration with contemporary digital music production, MIDI sequencing and studio software in wide use by the industry. Says Kyle Simpson, D.M., associate professor of commercial media composition: “Our media composition students gain hands-on education and real-world experience in the film, TV and video game industries through a robust internship program where they work with professional composers and orchestrators. They also have opportunities to record their original scores with fellow CSUN students and L.A. studio professionals at some of the region’s most prestigious recording studios.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Diane Warren (multiple Oscar-nominated songwriter); Pinar Toprak (Captain Marvel)

UNT teaches visual media scoring and composition through its Division of Composition Studies in the College of Music and its Department of Media Arts. Music Composition & Media Scoring features a Master of Arts in music composition with a specialized media composition track, in addition to general computer music and interdisciplinary paths. Composition majors collaborate with student filmmakers and instrumental ensembles and present original compositions through workshops, reading sessions and the Spectrum concert series. Students also can work with cable TV station ntTV and radio station KNTU-FM on audio production, sound design and screen media.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Norah Jones (Grammy-winning musician); Don Henley (The Eagles)

#758. This AI ‘mechanic’ can peer inside the black box of other neural networks

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Some AI models behave like mechanics — fixing issues in other models that they neither designed nor fully understand. Credit: Mint Images/Getty

Researchers have used an artificial-intelligence model to read and tinker with the internal workings of another AI network — offering a new way to peek into the ‘black box’ of AI.

Computer scientists usually improve models by training them in tiny increments or by building them from scratch. A team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge has demonstrated how an AI model called GPT-6 Astra can interpret the raw internal values of some other models well enough to predict what different parts of the systems do. It can then edit the models to make improvements — including boosting their mathematical abilities. The authors reported their findings in a preprint1 on 2 November.

ChatGPT is a black box: how AI research can break it open

ChatGPT is a black box: how AI research can break it open

Frontier AI models are “showing early sparks” of an ability to treat neural networks like files that they can read, reason about and change, says co-author Rikiya Takehi, a machine-learning researcher at MIT.

The results do not mean that Astra, developed by OpenAI in San Francisco, California, can explain or understand how a given AI network works. But the findings suggest that general-purpose AI models — such as ChatGPT or Claude — might be able to modify a network in useful ways, like a mechanic who can identify and fix issues in an engine that they neither designed nor fully understand.

Researchers already try to interpret how different components of a network create its outputs. The preprint shows that it is possible to automate some of these ‘interpretability’ methods, says Fazl Barez, an AI-safety researcher at the University of Oxford, UK.

Researchers hope that better understanding models in this way will help to create safer AI systems, although Barez cautions that this assumption is “largely untested”.

It remains unclear if Astra is going beyond applying information and techniques learned in its training. Barez says he would be surprised if Astra is able to read and interpret models in ways that go beyond existing human abilities.

Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be

Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be

Still, if developed further, such ability to reprogram models might be an asset in developing AI for science, says Marinka Zitnik, a computer scientist and bioinformatician at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. For example, it could help to spot errors in a model ahead of real-world testing, she says.

Frontier AI systems are based on massive neural networks — brain-inspired architectures in which layers of processing units, or neurons, are linked by billions of ‘weights’, values that represent the strength of connections inside a model. The strength of each weight is slowly nudged during training to make the model better at, for example, predicting a protein structure or the next word in a sentence.

The complex way in which a model’s features link to its outputs means they are often described as black boxes. Interpretability researchers run experiments to work out, for example, which weights are activated under specific conditions. Researchers have also previously developed custom models that can learn to edit other models2.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03679-8

Takehi, R., Teoh, J., Zhang, A. & Khattab, O. Preprint at alphaXiv https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.weight-space-programming (2026).

Schmidhuber, J. Neural Comput. 4, 131–139 (1992).

Philae drifted and bounced around the comet for two hours before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P. To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement.

The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired.

When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space. The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down.

Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it. Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.

The European Space Agency's Rosetta and Philae expedition was a first-of-its-kind mission, an endeavour to not just rendezvous with a comet and watch it change over time as it approached the sun (that was Rosetta's job), but also to soft-land a probe on its icy and rocky surface to see what a comet is truly made of.

The Rosetta and Philae mission succeeded on both counts, but Philae's historic landing was marred by its turbulent touchdown. Philae actually landed three different times on Comet 67/P, all because the harpoons designed to secure it in place didn't fire as planned.

After the first landing, Philae bounced up and drifted around the comet for two hours, making another bounce before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it. Scientists figured it was stuck in a shady spot where sunlight couldn't reach its solar panels. Because it was solar-powered, Philae needed to be facing the sun properly to generate enough power for sustained operation on the comet's surface.

Still, Philae did have some power stored in batteries, which lasted for more than two days on the surface. That allowed Philae to perform some science with its 10 instruments in the time it had on Comet 67/P. Most notably, Philae found organic molecules that had never been detected on a comet before.

The Rosetta orbiter continued to orbit Comet 67P until September 2016, and it was in that month -- just weeks before Rosetta itself landed on the comet on Sept. 30, 2016 -- that the spacecraft rediscovered the Philae lander lying on its side in a rocky crevice.

#756. Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images

The Milky Way is believed to contain billions of planets beyond our solar system. These distant worlds, known as exoplanets, offer astronomers an opportunity to explore other planetary systems, identify potentially habitable environments, and perhaps eventually discover evidence of life elsewhere in the universe.

Finding these planets is one challenge. Actually seeing them is another. Most exoplanets orbit stars that shine so brightly that the planets become nearly impossible to distinguish from the surrounding glare. Even the most advanced space telescopes struggle to separate the faint light of a distant planet from the overwhelming brightness of its host star.

Now, researchers have developed a powerful new method for removing that starlight from telescope images, revealing planets that were previously hidden. The technique uses a sophisticated computer simulation of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and has already exposed an exoplanet that was concealed in existing observations. In tests involving known planets, it achieved two to 15 times greater detection sensitivity than conventional approaches.

A Digital Twin of James Webb Reveals Hidden Planets

The breakthrough centers on a virtual replica of Webb's Near Infrared Camera (NIRCam), an instrument designed to observe the universe in infrared light. By recreating how the camera operates, researchers can identify and correct tiny imperfections that interfere with its observations.

The virtual model, often called a "digital twin," allows scientists to simulate the telescope's behavior and determine how starlight spreads through its optical system. Once they understand the patterns produced by the star, they can digitally subtract much of that glare, making faint planets easier to detect.

"Directly imaging exoplanets is incredibly challenging because even the tiniest imperfections in a telescope can make it difficult to separate the faint light of a planet from the overwhelming glare of its star," explains Caltech's Katie Bouman, professor of computing and mathematical sciences, electrical engineering and astronomy, a Rosenberg Scholar, and a Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator, who is a co-author of a Nature paper about the new method published online November 4.

"What's exciting is that we're showing how computation can help overcome limitations of the telescope itself," Bouman continues. "By combining a physical model of the instrument with optimization techniques from machine learning, we have been able to remove starlight much more precisely, making it easier to detect faint exoplanets and even reveal one that was previously hidden in the JWST data."

How Scientists Make Blinding Starlight Disappear

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP). Rather than relying entirely on improvements to telescope hardware, the system uses advanced computation to correct problems in images that have already been collected.

To develop FLIP, the team created a detailed physical model of Webb's infrared camera. They then used computational techniques to examine millions of possible imperfections, subtle changes, and other unknown factors that could influence the telescope's observations.

These small variations matter because even an extremely slight distortion can alter how a star appears in an image. When astronomers attempt to remove the star's light, any remaining glare can overwhelm the much dimmer signal from a nearby planet.

By accounting for these effects, FLIP produces a highly precise model of the star's appearance. Researchers can then subtract that modeled starlight from the original observations, allowing previously obscured objects to become visible.

"This is the first time that we have demonstrated that these little imperfections or instabilities are not a limiting factor in the kinds of planets we can image," says lead author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, a graduate student at Northwestern University in the lab of astronomer Jason Wang, who is also a co-author of the paper. "As you go through this iterative process of trying to find what the telescope actually is doing during observations, you basically see the glare of the star disappearing in very bizarre ways. It gets dimmer and very deformed until at the end you get a pretty clean image and, if you're lucky, there's a blob there, which is a glowing planet."

A Failed Experiment Led to a Major Breakthrough

The idea behind FLIP began taking shape when Ferrer-Chavez was an undergraduate student at the Autonomous University of Yucatán in Mexico. He had already participated in a Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship project with Wang, who was then a 51 Pegasi b Postdoctoral Fellow (named after the first exoplanet discovered orbiting a Sun-like star) in the laboratory of Dimitri Mawet.

Mawet is the David Morrisroe Professor of Astronomy at Caltech and a senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed by Caltech. He also serves as director of instrumentation for the Caltech Optical Observatories.

At the time, Ferrer-Chavez was looking for additional opportunities to pursue research. Meanwhile, Wang had been discussing a potential collaboration with Bouman that would combine her expertise in computational imaging with his knowledge of astronomical instruments. Their shared goal was to improve the ability of telescopes to directly image exoplanets.

The two researchers brought Ferrer-Chavez into the project and began mentoring him. However, the initial effort did not produce the results they had hoped for.

"Rodrigo's senior thesis was an exploration of possible approaches, none of which ended up being what we did for this paper, but it helped rule out what not to do and also helped us understand the problem better," Wang says. "I believe our recent success was only possible because we did that exercise first."

Ferrer-Chavez originally attempted to train machine learning models to predict the patterns of starlight appearing in telescope data. That strategy proved unsuccessful, prompting the team to rethink how the technology could be used.

Instead of asking artificial intelligence to predict what the glare should look like, they turned to computational tools developed for machine learning to perform detailed physical calculations.

These methods allowed the researchers to adjust millions of variables, much like turning an enormous collection of control knobs. Each adjustment helped refine their simulation of the telescope until it more closely reproduced the actual observations. Performing this many calculations manually would be impractical.

The resulting approach combines the physical laws governing light and telescope optics with the computational power of modern optimization methods. Rather than simply guessing what should be removed from an image, FLIP uses a model of how the telescope produces that image in the first place.

James Webb's Archives May Contain More Hidden Worlds

One of the most exciting possibilities is that astronomers may not need new telescope observations to benefit from the discovery.

Webb has already collected enormous amounts of astronomical data, including images of stars that could harbor planets too faint to detect using earlier analysis methods. FLIP offers a way to revisit these observations and search for objects that were overlooked.

"We now have a tool that lets us discover and study planets that we were not able to 'see' before, even if that planet was already in an image in the JWST archive," Ferrer-Chavez explains. "We can try to find planets that may have been missed there, and also planets that perhaps we tried to image, but we could not actually detect at the time."

This means some planets that were previously considered beyond the reach of direct imaging could potentially be identified without sending another telescope into space.

It also changes how astronomers can think about existing observations. An image that appears to contain nothing but a brilliant star may hold additional information about planets hidden beneath its glare.

Pushing Telescopes Beyond Their Physical Limits

Astronomers have spent decades developing technology to reduce the overwhelming brightness of stars. One important tool is a coronagraph, an instrument designed to block starlight so that faint objects nearby can be observed more clearly.

For example, NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope carries a Coronagraph Instrument developed by researchers at Caltech, JPL, and IPAC (a science and data center for astronomy at Caltech). The instrument is specifically designed to suppress starlight and improve the direct imaging of exoplanets.

But even exceptionally precise telescope hardware has unavoidable limitations. Wang explains that physical instruments alone cannot match the level of correction achieved by FLIP when processing the images.

"The James Webb Space Telescope, which we demonstrated on, is optically stable to the nanometer level, which just sounds pretty awesome, but that's still limiting," he says. "We're excited because this technique is not limited specifically to JWST. Because of some very specific design, this technique could be used on any telescope."

A nanometer is one billionth of a meter, meaning Webb's optical system maintains extraordinary precision. Yet even disturbances on this incredibly small scale can interfere with the detection of planets next to bright stars.

FLIP offers a different way around that problem. Instead of requiring the telescope itself to eliminate every tiny imperfection, the technique mathematically accounts for those effects after the observations have been made.

The researchers now intend to refine FLIP and investigate how it could work with additional instruments, including the Roman Space Telescope and telescopes operating from Earth's surface.

A Powerful New Tool in the Search for Another Earth

The implications may extend well beyond today's observatories. The researchers believe their approach could help shape future space missions, particularly those designed to search for planets resembling Earth.

One major possibility is NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). The mission is intended to become the first telescope specifically designed to search for evidence of life on planets orbiting other stars.

A central objective would be to photograph Earth-like planets within the habitable zones of stars similar to our Sun. A habitable zone is the range of distances around a star where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on a planet's surface, assuming suitable atmospheric conditions.

But the technical challenge is enormous. An Earth-like planet orbiting a Sun-like star can be approximately 10 billion times fainter than the star itself, making the planet extraordinarily difficult to distinguish from the surrounding light.

"The goal of HWO is to find Earth-like planets and the habitable zones of Sun-like stars through a direct imaging method," Ferrer-Chavez says. "The engineering challenge of trying to image something that is around 10 billion times fainter than something right next to it is a brutal -- not just to clean the image but to build a telescope that can take that image."

FLIP could make that challenge more manageable. If astronomers can digitally remove more unwanted starlight after capturing an image, future telescope designs may not need to overcome every source of optical instability through hardware alone.

The approach could therefore give engineers greater flexibility while allowing astronomers to extract more information from the light their instruments collect.

"I feel we just unlocked a new frontier," Wang says. "We've now gone beyond the telescope stability limit for the first time with this new technique, and this new paradigm, I think, can be applied to every instrument that's trying to image exoplanets."

Bringing the Search for Alien Life Into Focus

For Bouman, the long-term ambition is much larger than simply finding more distant planets. Astronomers ultimately hope to obtain direct images of worlds resembling Earth and examine them for possible signs of life.

Reaching that goal will require major advances in telescope engineering, astronomical instruments, and image processing. But the new research demonstrates that some of the most important improvements may come from better ways of interpreting data rather than building increasingly precise hardware.

"There's still a long way to go, but this work shows how much more is possible when we combine advances in telescope technology with computational imaging," Bouman says. "Sometimes, the key to seeing something new isn't just building a better instrument but finding a better way to make sense of the light it collects."

The findings were published in Nature in a paper titled "Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit." Additional co-authors include William T. Freeman and Brandon Y. Feng of MIT, along with Laurent Pueyo and Marshall D. Perrin of the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore.

The research received support from the Space Telescope Science Institute, the Sloan Foundation, an Amazon AI4Science Discovery Award, and the National Science Foundation.

#755. Soho House Creator Nick Jones Is Reinventing the Hotel — Again

The hospitality pioneer is back with St. Clement, the U.K. capital’s buzziest launch of 2026, already attracting rock stars, film icons and the fashion set. Does it deliver on the hype?

“London didn’t need another hotel,” says Nick Jones, as we watch the Thames flow by St. Clement, his latest argument that perhaps it did. “But I think we’ve cut through here by doing things differently.”

It’s a familiar claim in luxury hospitality, but Jones has form. In 1995, he opened the original Soho House in the city’s creative district, pioneering a shabby-luxury aesthetic that became a blueprint for members’ clubs worldwide. Since he stepped down as CEO in 2022, the empire he built has weathered headlines about overcrowding, declining service and the difficulty of securing tables. But whatever its fortunes today, Jones transformed London’s social scene once. Can he do it again? Related Stories Movies Listen to the River! 'Arrow for a Stone Heart' Is a Poetic Hybrid Experience Told Through an Indigenous Lens Movies 'Fatherland' Wins Top Camerimage Prize as 'Wild Horse Nine' Nabs Audience Award

The buzz around St. Clement has been deafening, even before its official September launch. In July, the Rolling Stones hosted an album launch in the penthouse upstairs. A crowd of 100 or so VIPs — including Daniel Craig and Sacha Baron Cohen — pogoed to “You Can’t Always Get What You Want” before drinking cocktails on a balcony with a panorama spanning Big Ben to The Shard. There was a drone show.

The Serpentine Summer Party — a highlight of London’s arts scene calendar every year — had an afterparty here. Over London Fashion Week, Burberry pitched up for an official dinner. Paul Mescal and Stanley Tucci have both been spotted hanging out, and the gastronomic grandees have begun their descent too. As I tuck into a plate of freshly made pappardelle with a silky veal ragù in Café Clement ($40), I spot Financial Times critic Jay Rayner — irascible scourge of London chefs since the Soho House heyday — arching an eyebrow over the menu. Scrutiny will pick up considerably when Lunette, a rooftop restaurant helmed by Florence Knight in her first venture since Sessions Arts Club, opens in the fall.

The determination to be — as Jones puts it — “faff-free” is evident the moment you walk through the door of St. Clement. In the lobby, you’re immediately lulled by a hit of scented candle, a bespoke creation by Perfumer H. Massive tomes on Basquiat are piled by a crackling fire. Conspicuously absent is any kind of formal check-in. “Everything is done in advance on WhatsApp,” explains relationships director Serena Lightner, previously of Chiltern Firehouse. “You’re welcomed, given your key and brought straight to your room.” No stiff wait by a mahogany desk; no jet-lagged fumbling for your credit card. Rates range from $934 per night for a standard room to $5,765 for the Central River Loft.

Through a discreet door is Bobbi’s Bar, the hotel’s naughty corner. Here the exposed concrete and warm, if unexciting, shades of the rooms and corridors give way to dark wood paneling, glowering lamps and conspiratorial nooks and crannies, including a daybed. “I took out all the things that annoy me about hotels,” is how Jones describes his approach to St. Clement; this must have included not being able to get a nightcap, because Bobbi’s enjoys a rare 3 a.m. license. Rumors of impromptu piano sing-alongs suggest St. Clement has taken some inspiration from the vibiest London opening of last year — Guinness pilgrimage spot The Devonshire, over in Soho.

Just down the road is the Corner Shop. Another Jones creation, it’s an achingly hip deli-cum-café-cum-wine bar, with menu items handwritten on brown paper bags and artful arrangements of pomegranates and walnuts next to some tea bags with a price tag of $20. I’d never been to a café where patrons do the meerkat move you see at parties — looking over each other’s shoulders in case someone more impressive can be spotted — but this is meerkat manor.

“The staff are very relaxed,” Jones tells me — this is true, a waiter welcomes me with a gesture not far from a shoulder rub — “I want [St. Clement] to feel like home for people coming from New York and L.A.” With a 24-hour health club and spa — including a 25-meter pool flowing parallel to the Thames outside ­— due to open next year, there’s no doubt people traveling in and out of the city will find it a convenient as well as cool-to-be-seen-at spot. For now, Jones insists there are no plans to expand beyond the neighborhood. “The great thing is there’s only one hotel,” he says with a grin. “I can know everyone by name.”
